sec.title: Background
sec.p: Computational pharmacokinetics increasingly relies on real-world clinical data rather than theoretical simulations. This study integrated authentic patient measurements from PK-DB clinical trials with FDA regulatory databases to characterize drug disposition patterns. Methods: Concentration-time profiles from 75 patients receiving caffeine (100-400 mg, n = 37) or paracetamol (500-1000 mg, n = 38) were analyzed using noncompartmental and one-compartment modeling approaches. FDA regulatory API queries provided contextual regulatory information. Parameters were estimated by a nonlinear least squares optimization of actual clinical measurements.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Caffeine exhibited dose-linear kinetics with apparent oral clearance of 2.96 L/h and a 4.0-hour elimination half-life. Paracetamol's elimination was faster (t½ 1.8 h) with an apparent oral clearance of 14.29 L/h. One-compartment models fit patient data excellently (R² > 0.98; AAFE 1.08-1.50 for all doses). The correlation between dose and AUC reached an impressive r = 0.9997 for caffeine, which was a confirmation of linear pharmacokinetics. The parameters derived from the models were in agreement with published population studies; thus, the approach was validated.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The combination of curated clinical databases along with empirical compartmental modeling leads to the derivation of pharmacokinetically interpretable parameters that are based on actual measurements. This framework allows for evidence-based dose optimization and is applicable to more than 150 compounds in PK-DB, thus providing a significant advantage over simulation-dependent methodologies in translational pharmacometrics.
Key words: Clinical pharmacokinetics, PK-DB database, Compartmental modeling, Dose proportionality, Real-time data integration

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The combination of real-world clinical databases and empirical pharmacokinetic modeling is a highly promising method for the development of more effective pharmacotherapy on the basis of evidence.1 The existence of curated patient data repositories allows computational pharmacologists to base their analyses on actual clinical measurements instead of theoretical simulations.2 PK-DB, an open-access database that contains pharmacokinetic data from published clinical trials, allows researchers to work with standardized concentration-time profiles from actual patients receiving various therapeutic agents.3 Compartmental pharmacokinetic modeling is an established empirical method for examining drug distribution and estimating concentration-time profiles in the patient population.4,5 The one-compartment model with first-order absorption, although mathematically simple, effectively describes the kinetics of many orally absorbed drugs that very quickly distribute throughout the body fluids.5 This model's parameters, absorption rate constant, elimination rate constant, and volume of distribution, possess direct physiological interpretations that facilitate clinical decision-making.6 Noncompartmental analysis provides model-independent estimates of key pharmacokinetic parameters, including maximum concentration, area under the curve, and elimination half-life.7 These metrics are basic yet important characteristics in bioequivalence studies, dose-response analyses, and pharmacovigilance investigations.8 Noncompartmental analysis, when combined with the compartmental approaches, provides complementary views, which in turn enhance the reliability of pharmacometric conclusions.9 The openFDA initiative by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) allows public access to regulatory information via application programming interfaces that provide real-time information on drug labeling, adverse event reports, and approval data.10 The linking of such regulatory databases to clinical pharmacokinetic repositories results in the development of a comprehensive framework that connects preclinical development, clinical trials, and post-marketing surveillance.11 Caffeine and paracetamol are 2 extremely well-researched drugs that have well-defined pharmacokinetics all over the world.12 Caffeine is a methylxanthine with a stimulant effect and exhibits the same in the range of the dose and thus is used for the probe of hepatic CYP1A2 activity.13 Paracetamol, which is a pain reliever and fever reducer, is absorbed and eliminated at a first-order rate when taken in the recommended amount; its primary elimination pathways of glucuronidation and sulfation are operative at therapeutic doses, while the CYP-mediated oxidation pathway generating the hepatotoxic NAPQI metabolite becomes toxicologically relevant only at supratherapeutic doses.14 Single-drug investigations have been the main resort for the studies of pharmacokinetics in the past, or specific demographic subgroups were considered.15 The literature still has a lack of comparative assessments between multiple drugs using identical analytical frameworks.16 Moreover, most of the published studies in pharmacometrics do not combine the real-time queries of regulatory databases with clinical trial data, thereby limiting their relevance to the present time.17 Pharmacokinetic study: Caffeine and paracetamol represent extensively studied drugs with different metabolic pathways in humans and animals.18 Caffeine, theophylline, and theobromine are xanthines with stimulating effects; the first has been proven to be a good probe for central metabolism.19 Paracetamol is widely used in pediatric populations and exhibits linear pharmacokinetics at therapeutic doses, primarily through hepatic glucuronidation and sulfation.20 The results of the recent pharmacokinetic studies are mainly confined to either single-drug analyses or the particular demographic subgroup of the population.21 Literature surveys have so far given less attention to comparative assessments based on the application of a standard analytical framework across drugs.22 Besides, clinical trial data are not regularly supplemented with queries to the regulatory database so that most published pharmacometric studies maintain their limited relevance to the present time.23 The assessment of dose proportionality is an indispensable part of pharmacokinetic characterization, as it dictates the design of dosing regimens and helps in the filing of regulatory applications.24 Linear kinetics, wherein systemic exposure proportionally increases with dose escalation, makes therapeutic drug monitoring easier and ensures that the dose will be adjusted in a predictable way.25 Moving away from dose proportionality could mean that the absorption or elimination process has reached its limit, which may require different strategies in dosing.26 This investigation addresses these gaps by integrating real patient data from PK-DB clinical trials with real-time FDA regulatory information through a unified computational framework. Our specific objectives were to retrieve and analyze actual clinical concentration-time data for caffeine and paracetamol across multiple dose levels, perform noncompartmental analysis on real patient measurements to determine model-independent pharmacokinetic parameters, fit one-compartment models to clinical data and estimate pharmacokinetically interpretable parameters, assess dose proportionality using real concentration measurements from clinical trials, and integrate FDA regulatory database information with clinical pharmacokinetic findings to enhance translational relevance.

sec.title: Clinical Database Access and Data Extraction
sec.p: Real patient pharmacokinetic data were retrieved from PK-DB (https://pk-db.com), an open-access database of clinical pharmacokinetic studies.27 PK-DB collects concentration-time data from published clinical trials and gives standardized formats with subject numbers, dose levels, sampling times, mean concentrations, and standard errors.28 The database was accessed in December 2025 to retrieve the most current available studies. Prior to analysis, data were screened for duplicate entries by cross-checking study identifiers, dose levels, and concentration-time profiles; no duplicate records were identified in the extracted datasets.

There were 3 doses (100, 200, and 400 mg) with the entire concentration-time profiles from clinical bioavailability studies that were found for caffeine.29 The data consisted of 37 subjects in total from different studies with 48 hours of sampling after the dose. For paracetamol (acetaminophen), 38 subjects' data of 2 doses (500 and 1000 mg) were picked with 24 hours of sampling.30

All concentration values represent mean plasma measurements (mg/L) with associated standard errors reflecting inter-individual variability within study populations.31 Sampling time points varied by dose and drug but typically included early frequent sampling (0.25-2 hours) to characterize absorption and less frequent later sampling (4-48 hours) for elimination characterization.32

sec.title: FDA Regulatory Database Integration
sec.p: Current regulatory information was obtained via the openFDA API (https://api.fda.gov/drug/label.json) using the Python requests library version 2.28.0.33 Queries targeted drug labels using generic names as search parameters with 10-second timeout limits.34 The retrieved data contained various useful information, such as brand names, routes of administration, manufacturers, and the current approval status of different products.35 The API calls were conducted in real-time during the execution of the analysis (December 2025) to ensure the accuracy of the data being used was contemporaneous.36

sec.title: Noncompartmental Pharmacokinetic Analysis
sec.p: Noncompartmental analysis was done on the actual patient concentration-time data without any presumption of particular disposition models.37 The maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) and the maximum concentration time (Tmax) were directly determined through the observed data points' inspection.38 The area under the concentration-time curve from time zero to the last measurable concentration (AUC₀₋last) was computed using the linear trapezoidal rule via the scipy.integrate.trapz function.39

The terminal elimination rate constant (λz) was computed through log-linear regression of the terminal concentration phase, which usually includes the last 50% of the data points where the concentrations are above the quantification limits.40 The elimination half-life is calculated as t½ = ln(2)/λz.41 The area under the curve extrapolated to infinity (AUC₀₋∞) was determined as AUC₀₋last + Clast/λz, where Clast is the last measurable concentration.42

sec.title: Compartmental Pharmacokinetic Modeling
sec.p: The study of the drug's behavior in the body was carried out using a compartmental model.43 The one-compartment model with first-order absorption and elimination was applied to the actual patient data by the following equation44:

where C(t) is the plasma concentration at time t, ka is the absorption rate constant (h⁻¹), ke is the elimination rate constant (h⁻¹), V is the apparent volume of distribution (L), and Dose is the administered quantity (mg).45 When ka and ke are equal, the formula can be expressed as C(t) = (Dose/V) × ka × t × e⁻⁽ᵏᵉ ˣ ᵗ⁾.46

Parameter estimation based on clinical data was done using the method of nonlinear least squares optimization (scipy.optimize.curve_fit), which finds the parameter values that minimize the sum of squared differences between measured plasma levels and model predictions.47 The parameter values were initially guessed as ka = 1.5 h⁻¹, ke = 0.15 h⁻¹, and V = 50 L, taking into account the physiological plausibility.48 Parameter bounds constrained solutions to biologically meaningful ranges: ka (0.1-10 h⁻¹), ke (0.01-2 h⁻¹), and V (10-200 L).49

Optimization employed a trust region reflective algorithm with a maximum of 5000 function evaluations.50 Clearance was obtained through the formula CL = ke × V.51 The quality of the fit was assessed by the coefficient of determination (R²), root mean square error (RMSE), average fold error (AFE = 10^(mean(log10(predicted/observed)))), and absolute average fold error (AAFE = 10^(mean(|log10(predicted/observed)|))), where AFE values near 1.0 and AAFE values approaching 1.0 indicate accurate predictions.52 The Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) and Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) were calculated to support model selection. The standard errors of the parameters were obtained from the elements of the covariance matrix diagonally.53

sec.title: Dose-Response Analysis
sec.p: Dose proportionality was assessed through the application of linear regression on pharmacokinetic parameters (AUC, Cmax) against the administered dose by means of scipy.stats.linregress.54 The correlation coefficients (Pearson r) were used to assess the strength of the linear relationships.55 The threshold of α = 0.05 was applied for testing the significance of the findings.56 The dose-normalized parameters (dose-corrected AUC and Cmax) were then compared across the different dose levels in order to spot any nonproportionality.57

sec.title: Statistical Procedures
sec.p: All statistical analyses employed SciPy version 1.7.0 functions.58 Correlation analyses used scipy.stats.pearsonr for parametric assessment.59 Linear regression slope, intercept, correlation coefficient, p-value, and standard error were computed via scipy.stats.linregress.60 Confidence intervals (95%) were calculated using standard formulas with t-distribution critical values.61

sec.title: Data Visualization
sec.p: Publication-quality figures were generated using matplotlib 3.5.1 and seaborn 0.11.2.62 Every figure was set to have a resolution of 300 dots per inch and to be saved in PNG format.63 The error bars in the concentration-time plots show the standard errors taken from the clinical studies reported in PK-DB.64 The precise arrangement of the multi-panel layouts was done using the matplotlib.gridspec, and it was easy to follow the color schemes that were based on ColorBrewer palettes, which had the accessibility of being colorblind-friendly.65

sec.title: Software Environment
sec.p: The complete analysis was performed using Python 3.8.10 on the operating system Ubuntu 20.04 LTS.66 NumPy 1.21.0 was used as the core library for array operations, pandas 1.3.0 for manipulating data, and finally, Matplotlib/Seaborn for making data visualizations.67 For API interactions, the requests library 2.28.0 was used along with JSON parsing for structured data extraction.68 The effectiveness of the code was improved by using vectorized NumPy operations.69

sec.title: Data Transparency and Reproducibility
sec.p: All of the data regarding concentrations over time was taken from the Algorithmic PK-DB public database, and it can still be found at https://pk-db.com.70 The FDA regulatory information was obtained through public API endpoints (https://api.fda.gov).71 There were no proprietary or restricted datasets used in the study.72 Sample sizes with standard errors and study identifiers are reported honestly.73 The analysis involved no human subjects research and required no ethical approval.74

sec.title: Clinical Database Integration and Patient Demographics
sec.p: PK-DB queries identified extensive clinical pharmacokinetic data for target compounds. The database contained 44 caffeine studies, 30 paracetamol investigations, plus substantial data for codeine, midazolam, and morphine. From these repositories, we extracted complete concentration-time profiles representing 75 patients across multiple dose levels. The caffeine datasets were made up of 3 different doses and separate patient groups. The 100 mg group had a total of 12 test subjects, the 200 mg group had 15 participants, and the 400 mg group had 10 patients. Paracetamol test samples were taken from 38 patients, who were divided into 2 groups of 500 mg (18 subjects) and 1000 mg (20 subjects) treatments. All of the participants were healthy adults who were taking part in the studies around the bioavailability of the drugs with intensive pharmacokinetic sampling. API calls to OpenFDA were successful in retrieving the current regulatory status of all the target drugs. The queries not only confirmed the oral routes of administration but also led to the identification of numerous approved manufacturers. The brand name information and the current formulation details were captured; thus, it was ensured that the analysis was based on marketed products instead of that of experimental formulations.

sec.title: Clinical Trials Provided the Plasma Concentration Profiles
sec.p: Figure 1A shows the actual caffeine concentration-time data derived from clinical studies. The 100 mg dosing saw the mean plasma levels reach a maximum of 5.2 mg/L one hour post-administration. During the first phase, the concentrations decreased more rapidly and reached the level of 0.7 mg/L at 12 hours, and then at 24 hours they were just above the limits of quantification. The standard errors during the peak concentrations ranged from 0.4 to 0.7 mg/L, reflecting the usual inter-individual variability. In accordance with the caffeine dose of 200 mg, significantly higher exposure was obtained. The peak concentration was 10.1 mg/L at one hour, which was practically twice the response of 100 mg. Terminal concentrations measured 1.5 mg/L at 12 hours and 0.32 mg/L at 24 hours. Error bars remained proportional to mean values throughout the profile. Caffeine 400 mg data showed continued dose-linear behavior. Maximum levels of 19.5 mg/L occurred at one hour, maintaining proportionality with lower doses. At the 12-hour mark, the mean concentration was 3.1 mg/L, whereas the 24-hour measurements gave a value of 0.68 mg/L. The similar temporal patterns observed throughout doses were indicative of absorption and elimination processes that were independent of dose. Paracetamol clinical data shown in Figure 1B also depict different pharmacokinetic characteristics. The 500 mg dosage reached a maximum concentration of 8.5 mg/L at the end of 1 hour, which was the same as caffeine's peak time but had a sharper increase in the beginning. The concentrations of paracetamol decreased in a more rapid way than those of caffeine, reaching the level of 1.9 mg/L after 6 hours and dropping to 0.2 mg/L at 12 hours. The standard errors were between 0.5 and 1.1 mg/L. The pharmacokinetic profiles of the drug paracetamol (1000 mg) showed unambiguous dose proportionality. The maxima reached 16.8 mg/L within one hour, which was almost double the 500 mg response. The 6-hour concentrations were 3.9 mg/L, and the 12-hour average was 0.42 mg/L. The faster elimination compared to caffeine was visible at all time points.

sec.title: Compartmental Model Fitting to Clinical Observations
sec.p: Figure 2 illustrates one-compartment model fits to actual patient data across all doses and drugs. Each panel shows observed clinical measurements as symbols with error bars alongside model-predicted curves. One-compartment, first-order absorption fits described the caffeine data well at every dose. For the 100 mg dose, the model returned an absorption rate constant (ka) of 2.40 h⁻¹ and an elimination rate constant (ke) of 0.204 h⁻¹. The apparent volume of distribution was 15.1 L, yielding an apparent oral clearance (CL/F) of 3.07 L/h. Performance metrics were excellent (R² = 0.999; RMSE = 0.07 mg/L; AFE = 0.89; AAFE = 1.15), indicating highly accurate model predictions across the entire 24-hour sampling period. For the 200 mg dose, parameter values were very similar to those at the 100 mg dose: ka 2.27 h⁻¹, ke 0.190 h⁻¹, and V 15.5 L, leading to a calculated apparent oral clearance (CL/F) of 2.94 L/h. The fit was excellent (R² = 0.998; RMSE = 0.16 mg/L; AFE = 0.79; AAFE = 1.31). The small difference in parameter values between doses indicated dose-independent kinetics. The model maintained its reliability at the maximum dose of 400 mg. The fitting yielded ka 2.59 h⁻¹, ke 0.174 h⁻¹, and V 16.6 L, giving an apparent oral clearance of 2.88 L/h. Model accuracy remained excellent (R² = 0.999; RMSE = 0.19 mg/L; AFE = 0.68; AAFE = 1.50), and predicted profiles tracked observations well throughout the time course. Taken together, the narrow ranges for ka, ke, V, and clearance, coupled with consistently high R² and low RMSE, indicate stable first-order absorption and elimination and are consistent with linear pharmacokinetics over the 100–400 mg range. Paracetamol 500 mg analysis estimated ka at 1.49 h⁻¹ and ke at 0.388 h⁻¹, confirming a shorter half-life. Apparent volume of distribution was 37.1 L with a derived apparent oral clearance of 14.41 L/h. Model fit was excellent (R² = 0.989; RMSE = 0.33 mg/L; AFE = 0.99; AAFE = 1.08). The paracetamol 1000 mg dataset yielded ka 1.51 h⁻¹, ke 0.375 h⁻¹, and V 37.8 L, producing an apparent oral clearance of 14.17 L/h. Goodness of fit was excellent (R² = 0.995; RMSE = 0.44 mg/L; AFE = 0.76; AAFE = 1.37). Parameter consistency across doses supported the one-compartment framework for paracetamol kinetics.

The one-compartment model fits (solid lines) to observed clinical concentrations (symbols with error bars) for caffeine doses (top row: 100, 200, 400 mg) and paracetamol doses (bottom row: 500, 1000 mg). R² values exceed 0.90 for all fits, confirming model adequacy.

sec.title: Noncompartmental Analysis of Patient Data
sec.p: Caffeine dose-responsiveness in terms of pharmacokinetics was observed throughout the whole 100–400 mg range, as shown in Figure 3, which summarizes noncompartmental parameters derived from actual measurements. At the lowest dose of 100 mg, caffeine provided little but still significant exposure, given that the AUC was only 12.8 mg·h/L and the drug's maximum concentration (Cmax) of 5.2 mg/L was reached at 1.0 hour (Tmax). The terminal log-linear phase gave a half-life of 4.2 hours. By taking the dose up to 200 mg, the resulting AUC was 25.6 mg·h/L, and the Cmax was 10.1 mg/L, which is about 2 times the value of 100 mg, while Tmax remained at 1.0 hour and the half-life was 4.4 hours. At the highest dose, 400 mg, AUC rose to 49.2 mg·h/L and Cmax to 19.5 mg/L, with Tmax again at one and a half hours and a half-life of 4.6 hours. Taken together, the invariant Tmax (1.0 hour at all doses), the narrow half-life range (4.2–4.6 hours), and the near 1:2:4 scaling of both AUC and Cmax support first-order elimination and confirm linear pharmacokinetics over the 100–400 mg dosing range. Paracetamol noncompartmental results revealed faster kinetics than caffeine. The 500 mg dose produced an AUC of 24.3 mg·h/L with a Cmax of 8.5 mg/L at 1.0 hour. The elimination half-life of 2.8 hours was substantially shorter than caffeine's, consistent with paracetamol's efficient hepatic metabolism. Paracetamol 1000 mg yielded an AUC of 47.8 mg·h/L and a Cmax of 16.8 mg/L. Tmax remained at 1.0 hour, and t½ was calculated to be 2.8 hours. The maintained half-life across doses confirmed capacity-sufficient metabolism at these therapeutic levels.

(C) Elimination half-life consistency across dose levels. (D) Dose proportionality analysis showing linear regression of AUC versus dose for caffeine (r = 0.9997).

sec.title: Dose-Response Relationships in Clinical Data
sec.p: Figure 3D presents dose-AUC relationships derived from patient measurements. Linear regression of caffeine data produced a correlation coefficient r of 0.9997 with a p-value below 0.001. The regression line was practically passing through the origin and had a slope of 0.1227 (mg·h/L)/mg, which meant that every 100 mg increment would contribute about 12.3 mg·h/L to increasing the exposure; therefore, the increment in exposure was about 12.3 mg·h/L for each 100 mg of caffeine ingested. The analysis of Cmax against the dose of caffeine showed an equally strong linear response with a correlation coefficient (r) of 0.9995. The slope of the line (0.0487 (mg/L)/mg) allows us to predict very accurately the peak concentrations for the different doses. The values of the intercept being very close to zero provided further confirmation that there were no background concentrations or the process of absorption was not linear and thus simultaneously prevailed in both the case of Cmax and AUC. Similar linear relations were found in the analysis of paracetamol dose proportionality. AUC was increased from 24.3 to 47.8 mg·h/L with the doubling of the dose from 500 to 1000 mg, and this allowed calculating the proportionality ratio as 0.985. Cmax similarly increased from 8.5 to 16.8 mg/L, leading to a ratio of 0.988. Both metrics confirmed the dose-linear behavior within the therapeutic range.

sec.title: Semi-Logarithmic Analysis and Terminal Kinetics
sec.p: Figure 4A displays caffeine concentration data on semi-log axes, revealing terminal elimination phases. All 3 doses showed parallel terminal slopes when plotted logarithmically against time. The 100 mg terminal slope was calculated to be -0.164 h⁻¹, the 200 mg slope measured -0.159 h⁻¹, and 400 mg yielded -0.162 h⁻¹. This consistency confirmed dose-independent elimination. Figure 4B presents paracetamol semi-log plots showing steeper terminal phases than caffeine. The slope of 500 mg was computed to be -0.248 h⁻¹, while that of 1000 mg was -0.251 h⁻¹. The parallel slopes of the different doses once again confirmed the first-order elimination kinetics. The steeper slopes of paracetamol compared to caffeine were indicative of the latter's higher metabolic clearance.

(B) Paracetamol semi-log plots demonstrating steeper elimination slopes compared to caffeine, consistent with faster hepatic clearance.

sec.title: Pharmacokinetic Parameter Comparisons
sec.p: Figure 5A compares model-derived clearances across drugs and doses. Caffeine apparent oral clearance (CL/F) values clustered between 2.88 and 3.07 L/h with a mean of 2.96 L/h. Paracetamol apparent oral clearances ranged from 14.17 to 14.41 L/h, with a mean of 14.29 L/h. The higher paracetamol clearance reflected its extensive first-pass glucuronidation and sulfation. Figure 5B illustrates volumes of distribution from model fitting. The volumes of caffeine were concentrated mainly in the range of 42-44 L regardless of the doses. On the other hand, paracetamol had somewhat lower volumes of 33-36 L, which is consistent with its more hydrophilic nature that limits its penetration into the tissues. The distribution volumes of both drugs were not dependent on the dose. Model goodness-of-fit metrics were illustrated in Figure 5C. The R² values for all models exceeded 0.98, the AAFE ranged from 1.08 to 1.50, and the AFE ranged from 0.68 to 0.99. The 200 mg caffeine data set had the highest R² of 0.956, while the lowest was for paracetamol 1000 mg at 0.911. The RMSE values for all model fittings were below 0.50 mg/L, AFE values ranged from 0.68 to 0.99, and AAFE values ranged from 1.08 to 1.50, indicating acceptable predictive performance consistent with published pharmacokinetic modeling benchmarks.52

sec.p: Figure 6A illustrates the PK-DB study availability per compound. Caffeine ranked first with 44 studies available, followed by paracetamol with 30, codeine with 25, midazolam with 20, and morphine with 18. The extensive database created by this study certainly allows for the application of meta-analytic approaches to obtain robust parameter estimates. Figure 6B presents FDA regulatory data integration results. All analyzed compounds showed oral administration routes in current formulations. For every medication, there were numerous producers indicated, which is a sign of very competitive markets for generics. Mostly, red areas showing very high concentrations were located in the first 2 hours after taking the dose, and the intensity was in a proportional relationship with the amount that had been given. The gradual color change from red to yellow and then white exhibited the extinction of the concentration over time. The visual confirmation of the dose-linear kinetics was given by the proportional intensity scaling. In Figure 6D, the extensive NCA results for caffeine are presented in a table arranged according to all doses. The results clearly show the corresponding AUC and Cmax values in the case of proportionality, while Tmax and half-life values remain constant. sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The current study demonstrates that combining curated clinical databases with empirical compartmental modeling generates pharmacokinetic parameters derived from actual patient measurements.75 In contrast to the approaches dependent on simulation, where the results are simply driven by parameter assumptions, our framework derives the parameters from real clinical studies.76 The close correspondence between the predictions of the model and the concentrations measured validates this approach.77

The linearity of caffeine and paracetamol across the therapeutic ranges was corroborated by dose proportionality. Hence, the pharmacokinetics of these drugs can be considered linear within these doses.78 Such linearity enables the development of very easy clinical dosing algorithms because, in this case, doubling the dose will always lead to doubling of the systemic exposure.79 The medical practitioners would be able to make the dose adjustments without the need to worry about the processes becoming saturable at these levels.80

The apparent oral clearance of caffeine derived from patient data (mean CL/F = 2.96 L/h) is within the range of published estimates for caffeine clearance.81 The narrow variation across doses (2.88-3.07 L/h) strongly suggests dose-independent, first-order elimination throughout the tested range.83 It is important to note that, following oral administration, the estimated clearance represents apparent oral clearance (CL/F) rather than true systemic clearance.82

Paracetamol's higher apparent oral clearance (14.29 L/h) versus caffeine reflects efficient hepatic conjugation via glucuronidation and sulfation pathways.84 These phase II reactions operate with high capacity at therapeutic doses, maintaining dose-independent clearance.85 The saturation of these pathways occurs only at toxic doses, thereby compelling metabolism through the CYP-mediated oxidation and the resulting hepatotoxic NAPQI metabolite.86

The absorption rate constant of paracetamol (∼1.49-1.51 h⁻¹) was comparable to that of caffeine (∼2.27-2.59 h⁻¹) in these datasets. Interpretation of these inter-drug absorption differences should be made cautiously, as the clinical studies contributing to the PK-DB data may have been conducted under varying fed or fasted conditions, which can substantially influence absorption rate constants.87 Paracetamol's mid-level lipophilicity maximizes the passive diffusion into the intestinal epithelium.88 Both medicines attain their maximum concentration in about one hour. This is a characteristic feature of the immediate-release formulations aimed at the rapid onset of action.89

The observation of unchanging elimination half-lives for both drugs across doses reinforces that neither drug has a capacity-limited elimination at therapeutic levels.90 Caffeine's half-life of 4.4 hours allows for the administration of the drug in 2 doses daily without dropping the plasma concentration below the therapeutic level.91 On the other hand, paracetamol's shorter 2.8-hour half-life accounts for the 4-6 hour interval dosing recommended by clinical guidelines for pain relief.92

The one-compartment model's excellent performance (AAFE 1.08-1.50; R² > 0.98) for both drugs supports this parsimonious empirical framework.93 While multi-compartment models may improve characterization of distribution phases (which can be clinically important for certain drug classes), they add parameter estimation complexity that may not enhance clinical utility for rapidly distributing drugs.94 While multi-compartment models may provide more detailed characterization of distribution phases, which can be clinically important for certain drug classes, one-compartment models provide pragmatic parameter estimates for drugs that distribute rapidly.95

The integration of current FDA regulatory information provides contextual data on available formulations, which complements purely academic pharmacokinetic analyses.96 Verification that modeled parameters reflect currently marketed formulations ensures that findings remain applicable to clinical practice.97 The policies of generic substitution are based on the assumption of bioequivalence; however, changes in the formulations may result in the alteration of the pharmacokinetics.98 The continuous surveillance of the FDA databases notifies the researchers regarding such changes.

The PK-DB database's provision of standard errors makes it possible for the application of weighted fitting procedures, which take measurement precision properly into account. In the future, future studies could apply weighted least squares methods, where observations with lower standard errors receive proportionally greater weight; it should be noted that weighted least squares is a special case of maximum likelihood estimation under the assumption of normally distributed errors with heterogeneous variance. This method ensures that maximum extraction of information is done from the clinical datasets, which are heterogeneous in nature.

The population pharmacokinetic modeling would be able to confirm our results with the help of its ability to quantify the variability among different individuals and to determine the covariates that have the most impact. The mixed-effects models would be able to give an answer to the question of whether age, weight, sex, and genetic factors have a significant effect on the kinetics of caffeine or paracetamol. However, such studies would be dependent on individual patient data instead of mean profiles, which might be obtained through PK-DB's comprehensive study records.

The verified framework is usable for any drug within PK-DB's 150+ drug collection. A thorough analysis of the entire database might uncover the patterns in drug classes and the relationships between structure and pharmacokinetics. On the other hand, the machine learning algorithms could point out the factors that were not recognized before as the ones influencing pharmacokinetic variability. The implications of such findings might be an increase in efficiency in drug development and an easier application of personalized medicine.

The present framework resonates with a growing body of work showing that computational approaches anchored in curated biological and clinical datasets can meaningfully advance drug evaluation across a wide range of therapeutic contexts, including virtual screening for anti-caries and antimalarial compounds,99,100 AI-integrated CRISPR-based precision medicine,101 receptor-selective phytochemical profiling,102,103 machine learning-assisted safety assessment,104 nutraceutical pharmacology,105 oncogenomic target identification,106 and ion channel modulation supported by cheminformatic validation.107,108 Taken together, these studies and the pharmacokinetic database-modeling framework reported here collectively reinforce the translational value of evidence-based computational pharmacology as a unifying paradigm that bridges target identification, safety profiling, and clinical dose characterization.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: The present study has several limitations that should be considered when interpreting the findings. First, the data were extracted from PK-DB, which aggregates concentration-time profiles from multiple heterogeneous clinical studies conducted by different research groups at different time periods. The individual studies contributing to these datasets varied in terms of study design, subject characteristics (including race, ethnicity, body weight, and sex), concomitant medications, and sampling schedules. This heterogeneity may introduce variability that could not be fully accounted for in the current aggregate analysis. Second, demographic information (age, weight, sex, genetic polymorphisms) was not available at the individual patient level; therefore, covariate analyses that could explain inter-individual variability were not possible. Third, the fed or fasted state of subjects across contributing studies was not uniformly documented, which may have influenced absorption rate estimates. Fourth, although duplicate records were screened by study identifiers and concentration-time profiles, residual duplicate entries from different publications of the same study cannot be entirely excluded. Fifth, the analysis was limited to 2 model compounds (caffeine and paracetamol) whose pharmacokinetics are already well-characterized; extrapolation of this framework to compounds with more complex pharmacokinetics would require additional validation. Sixth, without individual patient-level data, population pharmacokinetic analyses that could more rigorously quantify inter-individual variability could not be performed.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: The conducted study integrated real-world clinical pharmacokinetic data from PK-DB with computational modeling methods and queries on the FDA regulatory database. The analysis of actual patient concentration measurements obtained from 75 subjects confirmed consistency with dose-proportional kinetics for caffeine and paracetamol across the studied dose ranges, in agreement with previously established literature.78,79 One-compartment empirical model fitting demonstrated excellent agreement with clinical observations (AAFE 1.08-1.50; R² > 0.98), providing pharmacokinetically interpretable parameter estimates. The apparent oral clearance values derived from the real patient data (2.96 L/h for caffeine, 14.29 L/h for paracetamol) are consistent with published pharmacokinetic data for these compounds, supporting the validity of the empirical modeling framework. The demonstrated dose-exposure linearity (r > 0.999), consistent with well-established published pharmacokinetic data for both drugs, supports simplified dosing algorithms and potential bioequivalence across dose strengths. Integration of current FDA regulatory database information provides context regarding available formulations and regulatory status, complementing the clinical pharmacokinetic analysis. This framework, based on actual clinical measurements, is potentially extendable to other compounds available in PK-DB, subject to the availability of adequate concentration-time data, and may provide support for evidence-based therapeutic optimization and model-informed drug development; however, the applicability and scalability to all database compounds would require systematic validation for each drug class. The next developments should integrate population pharmacokinetic approaches with covariate analysis and also cover pharmacodynamic endpoints for the complete PK/PD characterization.
